a11y.formula: 100 minus one penalty per failing rule, where penalty = base(impact) x min(1 + log10(nodes), 2), plus 10 if the keyboard crawl found a trap. Items axe marks as needing review are not scored.

items.label: Rating band E

carbon.formula: Grams CO2e per view (Sustainable Web Design v3, an estimate) placed in a rating band, then interpolated linearly inside that band, plus 3 for a green-hosted domain, capped at 100.

combined.formula: A weighted average of the accessibility and carbon scores, rounded to a whole number.

tradeoffs.title: Media that plays on its own
tradeoffs.a11y_impact: Motion that starts without being asked can trigger vestibular symptoms and pulls focus from the content. WCAG 2.2.2 expects anything moving for more than five seconds to be pausable.
tradeoffs.explanation: Autoplay is set on 1 media element. Replacing it with a poster image and visible controls saves about 1.00 MB (0.290 g CO2e per view, estimated) for every visitor who never presses play, and hands control of the motion back to the person using the page. A poster image plus controls downloads a few tens of kilobytes instead of the whole media file, and only for visitors who press play.

tradeoffs.title: Below-the-fold images loaded eagerly
tradeoffs.a11y_impact: Everything below the fold competes for bandwidth with the content in view, so the first screen takes longer to become readable and usable. That hurts most on slow connections and on devices where a screen reader is waiting for the page to settle.

Deferring them with loading=lazy saves about 723.3 KB (0.209 g CO2e per view, estimated) for a visitor who does not scroll that far, and lets the first screen finish sooner for everyone. These bytes are deferred rather than removed. A visitor who scrolls the whole page still downloads them; one who does not, never does.

tradeoffs.title: Text baked into images
tradeoffs.a11y_impact: Screen readers cannot read words that only exist as pixels. The text also cannot be resized, reflowed, selected, searched or translated, and it blurs at high zoom.

tradeoffs.explanation: Suspected text baked into the pixels of 2 images. Moving those words into real HTML saves about 376.1 KB (0.109 g CO2e per view, estimated), and at the same time makes them readable by screen readers, resizable, selectable and translatable. Both goals point the same way here. Real HTML text weighs a couple of kilobytes; the banner it replaces weighs orders of magnitude more.

tradeoffs.title: Third-party scripts and widgets
tradeoffs.a11y_impact: Widgets injected by another domain are outside your control: their focus order, labelling and contrast are whatever the vendor shipped, and they frequently trap keyboard focus or appear as unlabelled controls.
tradeoffs.explanation: This page makes 4 requests to 1 other registrable domain (localhost:8082). Removing or deferring that code saves about 10.3 KB (0.0030 g CO2e per view, estimated), and takes back control of markup you are accountable for but cannot edit. Third-party code often pulls further requests of its own, so the measured bytes are a floor rather than the full cost.

tradeoffs.title: Clickable elements that are not buttons
tradeoffs.a11y_impact: A div with an onclick handler is not focusable, is not announced as a control, and does not respond to Enter or Space. Keyboard and screen-reader users simply cannot operate it.

tradeoffs.explanation: This page has 8 clickable elements built from divs or spans rather than buttons or links. Swapping them for native elements makes the controls focusable, operable by Enter and Space, and announceable by screen readers, and lets the hand-written keyboard and focus code go (changes no transfer bytes). This one needs a developer: the markup change is not safe to automate. A native button brings focus handling, keyboard activation and roles for free, so the hand-written script that emulated them can go.

tradeoffs.title: Animation with no reduced-motion escape
tradeoffs.a11y_impact: People who get migraines, nausea or dizziness from movement have told the browser so through their operating system. Without a prefers-reduced-motion rule the page ignores them.
tradeoffs.explanation: This page carries 0 animation or transition rules and never checks prefers-reduced-motion, so the movement runs even for visitors whose operating system has asked for it to stop. Adding the media query is a few lines of CSS and gives those readers a still page. This one saves no transfer bytes. It saves processor and GPU work on the visitor's device, which is where the Sustainable Web Design model puts the majority of a page view's energy.

tradeoffs.title: Captions add bytes, and are worth them
tradeoffs.a11y_impact: Without captions, deaf and hard-of-hearing visitors get nothing from the video, and neither does anyone watching with the sound off, in a noisy place, or in a second language. WCAG 1.2.2 requires captions for prerecorded audio.
tradeoffs.explanation: No caption track on 1 video here. Adding one costs bytes rather than saving them, and the point of this card is to show how few. A WebVTT track is plain text: about 2.0 KB per video on our estimate, against 1.001 MB of video already being shipped. The page's video payload goes from 1.001 MB to 1.003 MB, an increase of 0.20%. That is the entire carbon cost of making the video usable by deaf and hard-of-hearing visitors, and it is a rounding error next to the media it describes. Captions also need writing, so this is a person's job rather than a generated fix. WebVTT is plain text. The estimate used here is 2 KB per video, which covers roughly a minute of dialogue; the real file depends on how much is said.

tradeoffs.title: Dark mode: energy saving versus readability
tradeoffs.a11y_impact: Genuinely split. People with photophobia, migraine or concussion recovery often need a dark theme to read at all. People with astigmatism and some low-vision conditions get halation, where light text on a dark field smears, and read a light theme far more easily. Neither group is a minority you can design away.
tradeoffs.explanation: This page has no prefers-color-scheme handling, so every visitor gets the light theme whatever their system asks for. A dark theme is a real trade-off rather than a straight win. On an OLED screen dark pixels draw measurably less power, and for readers with photophobia, migraine or light sensitivity a dark theme is the difference between reading the page and closing it. For readers with astigmatism, though, light text on a dark background halates and smears, and a forced dark theme makes the page harder to read, not easier. The resolution is not to pick a side: honour prefers-color-scheme so each visitor gets what their system already says they want, and add a visible toggle so anyone can override it. Use #121212 rather than pure black with off-white text near #E8E8E8; the softer contrast reduces halation while still meeting AA. Expect this to cost roughly 700 B of extra CSS and script, about 0.0002 g CO2e per view on the estimate, and to be worth it. Adding a theme costs bytes rather than saving them. The energy argument for dark mode is about OLED screens, where dark pixels draw less power, and that saving is on the visitor's device, not in transfer.

tradeoffs.title: Font subsetting versus the words people are called
tradeoffs.a11y_impact: A subset that drops a glyph does not fail loudly. The character falls back to a system font mid-word, or renders as a box, which is jarring to read and can make a name unreadable. Names with diacritics, currency symbols and any second script are the usual casualties.
tradeoffs.explanation: This page ships 4 font files totalling 204.5 KB, enough that subsetting will come up. Trimming unused weights and styles is safe and worth doing. Trimming character ranges is where the tension sits: a latin-only subset saves more bytes and then breaks the moment someone's name carries an accent, a price appears in a second currency, or a quotation arrives in another script, and the fallback happens silently mid-word. Cut weights first, keep the ranges your content and your readers' names actually use, and always declare a sensible system fallback so a missing glyph degrades rather than disappears. Dropping unused weights is a safe saving and the scanner's font_bloat detector already counts it. How much a character-range subset would save depends on which ranges the page truly needs, so no number is claimed here.

tradeoffs.title: Image compression versus zoom
tradeoffs.a11y_impact: WCAG 1.4.4 expects content to survive 200% zoom, and plenty of people browse at that magnification or on a 2x display. An image with no resolution headroom left turns to mush for exactly the readers who most need to enlarge it.
tradeoffs.explanation: Resolution headroom is already below 2x on 1 image, so the compression fix must skip those images. Downscaling an image to exactly its rendered size looks fine at 100% on a 1x screen and falls apart at 200% zoom or on any high-density display, which is precisely where readers with low vision are. Keep 2x the rendered width as the floor, take the saving on the genuinely oversized images instead, and accept zero bytes saved here. This finding exists to stop a saving being taken, not to claim one. Leaving these images alone costs nothing extra; downscaling them further would save bytes at a real cost to readability.
